name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,356

clue.text: New flag and rope for children’s game

indicators.note: Something made new is remade out of the same material, so the letters given are set out afresh.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A new flag and a length of rope bought so the children have something to play with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' does the shuffling, though it reads as the first word of a shopping list. Neither prop is a red herring by accident: the game wanted is played with no equipment at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Leapfrog is the playground game of vaulting over a stooping partner's back, played by children everywhere, so the definition names it by kind.

clue.text: Composer’s musical sense securing 50 grand

indicators.note: To secure something is to get it safely inside your grasp, so the word doing the securing closes round the letters that follow.

blocks.note: the ear is the sense that takes in music
L is fifty in Roman numerals
g = grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: A composer's good ear landing him fifty thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composer' with no nationality attached is usually an invitation to a short, famous surname. The money arrives as two separate scraps rather than one sum, fifty and a thousand lettered apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Elgar was an English composer of the late Romantic period, so the definition names his trade and leaves the wordplay to say which one.

clue.text: Innovator, one working to be accepted by nobleman

indicators.note: What is accepted by somebody is taken in, so the letters named go inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: a peer is a nobleman — a duke, earl or baron entitled to sit in the Lords
one written as the Roman numeral I
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: An inventive worker hoping a titled patron will take him up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working' is the switch sense — not toiling but turned on, the way a light is. The comma after the first word is the only join between definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A pioneer is the first to open up a field or a territory, and being first is exactly what makes someone an innovator.

clue.text: Regret scheme abandoned by society

indicators.note: To be abandoned by somebody is to have them walk out on you; the society here is the letter S, and that is the letter that goes.

blocks.note: a ruse is a scheme or dodge, here with its S walked out on it

explanation.surface: Wishing you had never hatched a plan that everyone else has now walked away from.
explanation.walkthrough: A ruse is a trick or a dodge, the everyday word the clue wants for 'scheme'. The answer is the verb — to rue the day — not the bitter garden herb spelt the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue a decision is to wish bitterly that you had not taken it, which is what regretting it amounts to.

clue.text: Sleep in outfit left at theatre in the end

indicators.note: The end of a word is where its final letter sits, so that closing letter alone is taken.

blocks.note: a get-up is an outfit, especially a showy or odd one
l = left
the word AT handing over its own two letters
the final letter of THEATRE

explanation.surface: Dozing off in the clothes you were left standing in outside the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sleep in' is the British phrase for staying in bed past your usual hour, not for nodding off fully dressed. 'At' gives its two letters untouched, which is easy to walk past in a four-part charade.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleeping in and getting up late are the same morning described from either end — the extra hour under the covers, or the hour you finally rise.

clue.text: Fool sent back English dessert

indicators.note: Something sent back travels the way it came, so the letters are read from the far end.

blocks.note: e = English
pud is short for pudding, the British word for the sweet course

explanation.surface: Someone sending an English pudding back to the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool is itself an English dessert — gooseberry fool, fruit folded through cream — so the definition and the pudding beside it are the same word twice over. Pud is everyday British for the sweet course.
explanation.definitionFit: A dupe is somebody who has been taken in, the noun sense of 'fool' meaning a gullible victim rather than an idiot.

clue.text: Brought round some pure vodka and port

indicators.note: To bring a thing round is to turn it about, so the letters found are read in the opposite direction.
Some of a thing is a part and not the whole, so a run of letters is taken out of the words that follow.

blocks.note: a run of five letters bridging puRE VODka

explanation.surface: A guest arriving with vodka and port for the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' is the harbour, not the fortified wine standing next to the vodka. The town wanted is the Channel crossing for Calais, twenty-one miles of water away.
explanation.definitionFit: Dover is the port on the Kent coast of England from which the Channel ferries sail, so the bare word 'port' names it by what the town is.

clue.text: Someone chasing prize money runs around university

indicators.note: To go around a thing is to surround it, so the letters already assembled close on the one that comes next.

blocks.note: the purse is the prize money put up for a boxing match or a horse race
r = runs, the scoring unit in cricket
u = university

explanation.surface: A man after the prize money sprinting round the campus.
explanation.walkthrough: The purse is the money a fighter or an owner takes home, not something carried in a handbag. R for runs comes off a cricket scorecard, where runs are the points scored with the bat.
explanation.definitionFit: A pursuer is whoever is giving chase, so the definition states the role in plain words rather than offering a synonym.

clue.text: Fail to notice Italian chap snubbing southern European

indicators.note: To snub somebody is to cut them dead; southern here is the letter S, and it is that letter which gets cut.

blocks.note: signor is the Italian for Mr or gentleman, here with its opening S cut away
e = European

explanation.surface: An Italian gentleman giving a southern European the cold shoulder.
explanation.walkthrough: Signor is how you address a man in Rome, and it is the whole of the wordplay's first piece. 'Southern European' is split down the middle: one word supplies a letter to throw away, the next a letter to keep.
explanation.definitionFit: To ignore something is to take no notice of it, so the definition describes the same act as a failure rather than a choice.

clue.text: Moving TV near pub

indicators.note: What is moving is no longer where it was, and letters no longer where they were are letters rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A television being shifted to somewhere near the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' reads as a description of what is happening to the television and is in fact the instruction. TV hands over both its letters as raw material rather than standing in for anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A tavern is an inn where drink is sold and served, the older word for what Britain now calls a pub.

clue.text: Insist on popular fast food order without sides

indicators.note: The sides of a word are the letters at either edge, and going without them leaves only what lies between.

blocks.note: a burger is the popular fast-food order, here stripped of the letter at each edge

explanation.surface: Demanding the usual burger with nothing served alongside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without sides' reads as a plain instruction at the counter — no fries, no slaw — and is really a direction to shave a letter off each end. The definition runs to two words, not just the first.
explanation.definitionFit: To urge a course of action is to press for it hard and repeatedly, which is what insisting on something comes to.

clue.text: Band suddenly appear bored by playing tour video, ultimately

indicators.note: To be bored by something is to have it drilled through you, so the letters that follow are driven into the middle of the word before.
What is ultimate comes last of all, so each word it governs gives up only its closing letter.

blocks.note: to pop up is to appear without warning
the closing letters of PLAYING, TOUR and VIDEO

explanation.surface: A band turning up out of nowhere, sick of sitting through footage of their own tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bored by' looks like the band's mood and is a drilling instruction. 'Ultimately' reaches back over all three words before it rather than just the one it touches, which is where the three letters come from.
explanation.definitionFit: A pop group is a band playing popular music, so 'Band' is the general word for the kind of outfit named.

clue.text: Tree from Haiti cops destroyed

indicators.note: A destroyed thing has been broken apart, and letters broken apart can be put back in any order at all.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Police in Haiti tearing down a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The tree wanted is a small one of the cashew family, grown across Iran and the Levant for its green nut. 'Destroyed' does the shuffling while the surface has the police doing the damage.
explanation.definitionFit: The pistachio is a small tree of the cashew family, so 'Tree' defines the plant itself rather than the green nut it is better known for.

clue.text: Printed documents in support of manuscript

blocks.note: to be for something is to be in support of it
MS is the standard written abbreviation for manuscript

explanation.surface: Paperwork backing up an author's handwritten draft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In support of' is three words giving three letters, a preposition rather than an instruction about where a piece belongs. The answer is the printed sheets you fill in, not shapes or figures.
explanation.definitionFit: A form is a printed sheet with blanks to be completed, so 'printed documents' names the plural in its everyday office sense.

clue.text: Red-faced drunk detained by FBI agent

indicators.note: Somebody detained by an officer is held inside, so the word named goes within the one after it.

blocks.note: a fed is American slang for a federal officer
a lush is a habitual heavy drinker

explanation.surface: A drunk sitting in the cells after being picked up by a federal officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' is the noun here, a person, rather than the adjective it looks like. A lush is a soak or a boozer, and a fed is what Americans call an FBI man.
explanation.definitionFit: A flushed face has reddened with rushing blood, from heat, drink or embarrassment, which is what calling somebody red-faced describes.

clue.text: Warning light from webcam — be ready

indicators.note: What comes from something is taken out of it, so a run of letters is lifted straight out of the words that follow.

blocks.note: a run of five letters bridging webcAM, BE and Ready

explanation.surface: Telling the webcam to stand by before a broadcast starts.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash sitting inside the hidden run is camouflage: letters take no notice of punctuation. On a British traffic light the middle lamp is the one meaning stop if you safely can.
explanation.definitionFit: Amber is the middle lamp of a traffic signal, shown between green and red to warn drivers that the light is about to change.

clue.text: Reinvented Belgian language

indicators.note: To reinvent a thing is to make it over out of the same parts, so the letters are put together in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A Belgian language being made over from scratch.
explanation.walkthrough: Belgium really does have three official languages, so 'Belgian language' reads as a genuine phrase rather than as fodder followed by definition. The tongue wanted is spoken in Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal.
explanation.definitionFit: Bengali is the language of Bangladesh and West Bengal, with some 230 million speakers, so the bare word 'language' is definition enough.

clue.text: Country certain to admit popular American

indicators.note: To admit somebody is to let them in through the door, so the letters that follow go inside the word before.

blocks.note: sure = certain, as in sure of the answer
in = popular, the adjective of 'the in crowd'
Am. is the written abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A country confident enough to let a well-liked American through the door.
explanation.walkthrough: Two short pieces go inside rather than one, which makes the gap in the middle hard to judge. 'In' here is the adjective meaning fashionable, not the preposition it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: Suriname is a small republic on the north-east coast of South America, once Dutch Guiana, so 'Country' defines it plainly.

clue.text: Son leaves Mediterranean island with little warmth

indicators.note: To leave is to walk out; the son here is the letter S, and that is the letter which departs from the word beside it.

blocks.note: Sicily is the large island off the toe of Italy, here without its opening S

explanation.surface: A son walking out on a coldly received family holiday in the Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: The island is the obvious one and gives up only its first letter, which is the cheapest kind of deletion to spot once you have the length. 'With little warmth' is an adverbial phrase, so the answer has to be an adverb too.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak or act icily is to do it with no warmth at all, the chill being of manner rather than temperature.

clue.text: Cold cuts a German returned in Mediterranean resort

indicators.note: To cut into something is to go into it, so the letter named is driven inside the word beside it.
Something returned comes back the way it went, so the word it marks is read backwards.

blocks.note: ein is the German for 'a', written here backwards
c = cold, the letter on the tap

explanation.surface: A German sending the cold cuts back at a resort on the Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold cuts' is a deli platter in the surface and two separate instructions underneath: a single letter, and what that letter does. The German word wanted is the indefinite article, the commonest word in the language.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice is the city on the French Riviera and the largest resort on France's Mediterranean coast, so the definition names it by type and by sea.

clue.text: Shell company starts to needlessly cause havoc

indicators.note: The start of a word is its opening letter, so each of the words that follow gives up only its first.

blocks.note: co. is the written short form of company
the opening letters of NEEDLESSLY, CAUSE and HAVOC

explanation.surface: A shell company setting out to wreak pointless destruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shell company' is a real phrase — a firm existing only on paper — and the clue splits it down the middle into definition and first piece. The shell wanted is the big spiral one you can blow like a horn.
explanation.definitionFit: A conch is the large spiral sea shell of a marine snail, the one sounded as a trumpet, so 'Shell' names it by kind.

clue.text: Rambling hikes with hot Arab leader

indicators.note: To ramble is to wander off without keeping to a path, and letters that wander do not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
h = hot, the letter on the tap, joined to the fodder

explanation.surface: Wandering walks taken in the company of a hot-tempered Arab ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rambling' earns its keep twice over, since a ramble is itself a hike — which is exactly why it slips past as the instruction. H for hot comes off the bathroom tap.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheikh is the head of an Arab tribe or family and the title carried by Gulf rulers, so 'Arab leader' names the office.

clue.text: Smart bachelor likely to shower

blocks.note: b = bachelor, from the degree, BA or BSc
a rainy day is one likely to bring showers

explanation.surface: A clever single man who looks set for a soaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shower' is weather, not washing, and 'likely to' belongs with it rather than serving as a link. Smart is wanted in its clever sense, not its well-dressed one.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody brainy has plenty of brains, which is what calling a person smart means when the word is about wits rather than tailoring.

clue.text: Save clumsy craft that’s capsized

indicators.note: A capsized boat has turned right over, so the letters it marks are read the other way up.

blocks.note: a tub is a slow, clumsy boat, written here backwards

explanation.surface: A cumbersome little boat that has gone over in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save' is the preposition meaning except — all save one — and not the rescue verb the capsizing invites. Capsizing suits both the boat and a down entry, where the letters turn end over end.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a preposition, 'save' means except, and the answer carries the same sense in 'no one but her', so the two swap freely.

clue.text: Nervous editor bordering on giggly

indicators.note: A border runs along the outside edge of a thing, so only the outermost letters of the word that follows are taken.

blocks.note: ed. is the standard short form of editor
the outer letters of GIGGLY

explanation.surface: A jumpy editor on the verge of the giggles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bordering on' reads as almost — the editor nearly laughing — and works as an instruction to take a word's outside letters. Both edges are wanted, not just the opening one.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody edgy is tense and ready to snap at any moment, which is the ordinary sense of nervous.

clue.text: Where in Paris drunk crosses river instantly

indicators.note: To cross a river is to get from one bank to the other, so the word ends up lying on both sides of the letter named.

blocks.note: où is the French for 'where', and Paris is where French is spoken
tight is British slang for drunk
r = river

explanation.surface: A drunk crossing the Seine somewhere in Paris without pausing for breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where in Paris' asks for the French word rather than a location, which is the standard way of calling for a foreign term. Tight for drunk is old British slang, still alive in 'tight as a tick'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something killed outright is killed instantly, the adverb meaning at once and completely rather than by degrees.
